newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian politician accused of expenses fraud.
newsitem.headline: Australian politician accused of expenses fraud.

text.p: Australian opposition leaders called on Monday for a police investigation into an independent senator found to have wrongly claimed 43 nights of parliamentary travel allowances.
The conservative government, which relies on senator Mal Colston for the passage of its economic reforms, was forced to defend the senator against Labor accusations of fraud.
"There is no evidence to corroborate the proposition of deliberate and systematic fraud," Communications Minister Richard Alston told the Senate.

Colston said the 43 nights of wrongly-claimed travel allowance stemmed from poor book-keeping in his office, but the Labor Party -- from which he defected in August -- said the excuse was unbelievable.
"You might believe up to six nights mistakenly claimed," Labor senator Robert Ray told the Senate after the release of an inquiry into Colston's expenses. "How can you believe 43?"
Labor senator John Faulkner urged Senate President Margaret Reid to send the information to the police.
"What we are dealing with here today is nothing less than deliberate and systematic abuse of Senator Colston's parliamentary entitlements," Faulkner said.
If Colston were convicted of fraud he would have to quit the Senate, crucially changing the balance of power in Canberra.

Prime Minister John Howard's ruling Liberal-National coalition depends on Colston because it is two votes short of a majority in the Senate and all the other senators, except Colston and another independent, are left-leaning.
Non-government parties rarely back the government's main economic reforms, such as budget cuts, asset sales and market deregulation.
So Colston's defection from Labor in August for the first time gave the government, elected in March 1996, a good shot at getting economic reforms through parliament.
Labor has a traditional hatred of defectors and gleefully seized on accusations of dishonesty against Colston when they emerged earlier this year.
First a former staff member accused Colston in an administrative tribunal of misusing some expense allowances and giving office jobs to relatives who did no work.
Then Labor pushed the question of his travel allowances, resulting in an inquiry, the results of which were tabled in parliament on Monday.
The inquiry checked Colston's claims for an overnight allowance in Canberra against airline and other travel records and found that on 43 nights he was not where he said he was.
Colston's secretary said she had not always kept good records, so the senator had sometimes claimed the wrong nights by mistake.
